exampleAnswers.title: Finding the Standard Matrix of a Dilation Given a Vector and its Image

question.text: A linear transformation $\mathbf{T}$ represents a dilation. Given that $\mathbf{v}=\begin{bmatrix} 60 \\ 144 \end{bmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v})=\begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 12 \end{bmatrix},$ what is the standard matrix of $\mathbf{T}?$
question.explanation:
We can write $\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v})$ as follows:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v})&=\begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 12 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{12}\cdot \begin{bmatrix} 60 \\ 144 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{12}\mathbf{v} \end{align*}

So we have $\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}) = \dfrac{1}{12}\mathbf{v},$ and so the linear transformation $\mathbf T$ is a dilation with scale factor $k = \dfrac{1}{12}.$

The matrix that represents a dilation of scale factor $k$ is given by \[ \begin{bmatrix} k & 0 \\ 0 & k \end{bmatrix}. \]

Therefore, the standard matrix of $\mathbf{T}$ is \[ T=\begin{bmatrix}\dfrac{1}{12} & 0 \\ 0 & \dfrac{1}{12} \end{bmatrix}. \]

question.explanation:
Recall that a dilation of scale factor $k$ is represented by the matrix \[ \begin{bmatrix} k & 0 \\ 0 & k \end{bmatrix}. \]

Here, we have $k=17.$ Therefore, the matrix represents a dilation with a scale factor of $17.$

example.title: Identifying the Linear Transformation Represented by a Matrix

question.text: What linear transformation $\mathbf T$ is represented by the matrix $ T = \begin{bmatrix} 0 &-1\\ -1 &0 \end{bmatrix}? $
question.explanation:
Consider the standard basis $\{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \}$ of the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the unit square spanned by the vectors, as shown below.

Now, we compute the images of $\{ \mathbf{i},\mathbf{j} \}$ under $T$, as follows:

\begin{align*} \mathbf{i}' &= \mathbf{T}(\mathbf{i}) = \begin{bmatrix} {\color{blue}0} & -1 \\ {\color{blue}-1} & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} {\color{blue}0} \\ {\color{blue}-1} \end{bmatrix} = -\mathbf{j} \\[5pt] \mathbf{j}' &= \mathbf{T}(\mathbf{j}) = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & {\color{red}-1} \\ -1 & {\color{red}0} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} {\color{red}-1} \\ {\color{red}0} \end{bmatrix} = -\mathbf{i} \end{align*}

As a result, we obtain the following image:

Therefore, the matrix represents a reflection in the line $y=-x.$
